title: Poisson's Ratio
short_intro: Poisson's ratio is defined as the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain in a stretched or compressed elastic wire or rod. It is a dimensionless and unitless quantity that characterizes the transverse deformation of an isotropic elastic material.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of lateral and longitudinal strain, formula for Poisson's ratio, limiting values of Poisson's ratio for isotropic elastic materials (-1 to 0.5), and basic numerical problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Interrelation between elastic constants (Young's modulus Y, Bulk modulus K, Rigidity modulus eta, and Poisson's ratio sigma), volume conservation under elastic deformation (sigma = 0.5), and theoretical derivations of strain components.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Origin
bullets: When a wire is subjected to a longitudinal tensile stress, it elongates in the direction of the applied force (longitudinal strain) and contracts in the transverse or lateral directions (lateral strain).
Poisson's ratio (σ) is mathematically defined as the negative ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain.

The negative sign is conventionally introduced to make the numerical value of Poisson's ratio positive for most ordinary materials, since a positive longitudinal strain (extension) produces a negative lateral strain (contraction).

concept_notes.heading: Limiting Values of Poisson's Ratio
bullets: For thermodynamically stable isotropic elastic materials, the theoretical lower limit of Poisson's ratio is -1 and the upper limit is 0.5.
A material with σ = 0.5 undergoes no change in volume during elastic deformation (incompressible materials like rubber).
Most common metals have Poisson's ratio values ranging between 0.25 and 0.35 (e.g., steel is approximately 0.28 to 0.30, and copper is about 0.33).

concept_notes.heading: Relation Among Elastic Constants
bullets: The elastic constants of an isotropic solid are interrelated, meaning any two independent constants completely define the elastic behavior of the material.
The fundamental relations connecting Young's modulus (Y), Bulk modulus (K), Rigidity modulus (η), and Poisson's ratio (σ) are Y = 3K(1 - 2σ) and Y = 2η(1 + σ).
Eliminating Y from these relations yields the compatibility equation connecting K, η, and σ.

concept_notes.heading: Volume Deformation and Lateral Contraction
bullets: Consider a rod of length L and radius r. Under a tensile force, the length becomes L + ΔL and the radius becomes r - Δr.
Longitudinal strain is given by ε_{long} = ΔL / L, and lateral strain is given by ε_{lat} = Δr / r.
The fractional change in volume can be expressed in terms of longitudinal strain and Poisson's ratio as ΔV / V = ε_{long}(1 - 2σ).

derivations.title: Relation between Y, η, and σ
derivations.conditions: Isotropic elastic medium under pure shear stress, resolved into principal tensile and compressive strains at 45 degrees.
steps: Consider a cube subjected to shear stress resulting in principal tensile strain ε = τ / η along one diagonal and compressive strain along the orthogonal diagonal.
Alternatively, express the strain of a diagonal of length L under tensile stress σ_0 as ε = σ_0 / Y.
Relate the strains along the orthogonal axes using Poisson's ratio: lateral strains contribute via -σε.
Equating the shear strain components to the directional Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio formulations yields the standard elasticity relation.

derivations.title: Relation between Y, K, and σ
derivations.conditions: Isotropic material subjected to uniform hydrostatic pressure leading to isotropic volumetric strain.
steps: Consider a cube of side length a subjected to equal tensile stresses P in all three orthogonal directions x, y, and z.
The total strain along any one axis, say x, due to stress in all three directions is given by ε_x = (P / Y) - (σP / Y) - (σP / Y) = (P / Y)(1 - 2\sigma).
The volumetric strain is the sum of linear strains along the three axes: ΔV / V = 3ε_x = (3P / Y)(1 - 2\sigma).
Using the definition of Bulk modulus K = P / (ΔV / V), substitute the volumetric strain expression to obtain Y in terms of K and σ.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lateral Strain vs Longitudinal Strain Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of lateral strain (Δr / r) on the y-axis against longitudinal strain (ΔL / L) on the x-axis passing through the origin with a negative slope.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The negative slope of the straight line directly gives the value of Poisson's ratio (σ). Linearity indicates obedience to Hooke's law in the elastic limit.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions asking to identify the slope or interpret the sign of transverse deformation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus / Optical Lever Method (Contextual)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing two wires (experimental and reference) suspended from a rigid support, equipped with a spirit level, micrometer screw gauge, and scale.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used for precise measurement of Young's modulus, which indirectly feeds into calculations involving Poisson's ratio when combined with lateral extensometers.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct factual questions regarding least count and experimental measurement techniques for elastic constants.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Volume Change vs Poisson's Ratio Indicator
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar chart or theoretical curve showing fractional volume change (ΔV/V) as a function of σ from -1 to 0.5 for a fixed longitudinal strain.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Clearly demonstrates that at σ = 0.5, volume change is zero (incompressible); for σ < 0.5, volume increases upon stretching (auxetic behavior for negative values).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual PGT questions on incompressible fluids and anomalous elastic behavior.

solved_numericals.question: A metal wire of length 2 m and radius 1 mm is stretched by a force. If the longitudinal strain produced is 0.001 and Poisson's ratio for the wire is 0.3, calculate the lateral strain and the change in radius.
solution_steps: Identify given data: longitudinal strain (ΔL / L) = 0.001, Poisson's ratio (σ) = 0.3, initial radius (r) = 1 mm = 10^-3 m.
Use the formula for Poisson's ratio: lateral strain (Δr / r) = - σ * (ΔL / L).
Calculate change in radius Δr = - 0.0003 * 10^-3 m = - 3 * 10^-7 m (- 3.0 * 10^-4 mm).
solved_numericals.answer: Lateral strain = -0.0003; Change in radius = -3 * 10^-7 m (contraction)

solved_numericals.question: For a given isotropic material, the Young's modulus is 1.2 * 10^11 N/m² and the Rigidity modulus is 4.5 * 10^10 N/m². Find the Poisson's ratio and the Bulk modulus of the material.
solution_steps: Use the relation connecting Y, η, and σ: Y = 2η(1 + σ).
Use the relation connecting Y, K, and σ: Y = 3K(1 - 2σ).
Substitute Y and σ to find K: 1.2 * 10^11 = 3K * (1 - 2*(1/3)) = 3K * (1/3) = K.

solved_numericals.question: Prove that for an incompressible material, the Poisson's ratio is equal to 0.5.
solution_steps: Write the expression for fractional change in volume: ΔV / V = (ΔL / L)(1 - 2σ).
For an incompressible material, the volume remains constant during deformation, meaning ΔV = 0.
Set the fractional volume change to zero: (ΔL / L)(1 - 2σ) = 0.
Since the longitudinal strain (ΔL / L) is non-zero for active stretching, the term (1 - 2σ) must equal zero.

assumptions_and_limitations: The material is assumed to be perfectly homogeneous and isotropic, meaning its elastic properties are identical in all directions.
The deformations considered are strictly within the elastic limit where Hooke's law is valid and strains are very small (ε << 1).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poisson's ratio can have any positive value greater than zero without restriction.
common_misconceptions.correct: Poisson's ratio for stable isotropic solids is theoretically restricted between -1 and 0.5.
common_misconceptions.why: Exceeding 0.5 would imply a negative bulk modulus, leading to thermodynamic instability where compression increases volume.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poisson's ratio has units of strain (or meters).
common_misconceptions.why: It is defined as the ratio of two similar quantities (lateral strain to longitudinal strain), both of which are dimensionless ratios.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A negative Poisson's ratio is physically impossible.
common_misconceptions.correct: Materials with negative Poisson's ratio (auxetic materials) expand laterally when stretched.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermodynamic limits permit values down to -1, and specific microstructures exhibit auxetic behavior.

quick_revision: Poisson's ratio σ is the negative ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain, lying strictly between -1 and 0.5 for isotropic elastic solids.
Poisson's Ratio Definition: \sigma = - \frac{\Delta r / r}{\Delta L / L}
